description: We are Narayani Sena: Manthan Singh Rauthan and Shivam Joshi. We love Mars, maps and making exploration safer. Our project, Martian Map, is an EVA navigator built on real NASA data. It plans a Marswalk over 1 m HiRISE terrain in Gale and Jezero craters, steers around steep ground, sand and boulders, tracks the suit's oxygen and gives GO or NO-GO with reasons. A 3D helmet view always shows the way home. We work in Python, React and Godot. Skills we'd welcome: Mars geology and UX testing.
summary:
Martian Map is a map an astronaut can walk with: a Marswalk planner and navigator built on real NASA data for two real sites, the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, which Curiosity studied in 2025, and Perseverance's Three Forks sample depot in Jezero crater.

The crew picks a habitat and science stops. Martian Map routes the walk over 1 m HiRISE terrain, around steep, rough and sandy ground and the boulders our own detector finds in 25 cm HiRISE images. It simulates the suit's oxygen, battery, CO₂ scrubber and cooling water minute by minute, checks sunlight, weather, radiation, NASA DONKI space weather and radio coverage, and gives GO or NO-GO with the reasons. The plan then goes out with the crew: a web planner for the habitat, a 3D console with a first-person helmet HUD, and a printable traverse sheet and cuff checklist.

Mars Trek and the USGS-NASA geologic maps show Mars region by region; a crew on foot needs one small patch of ground, metre by metre. Martian Map layers data from five NASA missions (MRO, Mars Odyssey, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity) and all eight kinds of data the challenge names, from orbital minerals to rover laser chemistry and ground radar. Because crew safety comes first, every plan also shows every way home, says where its data may be wrong, and keeps working when something breaks.
details:
What it does

Martian Map plans a Marswalk (EVA) on real terrain, checks it for safety, and carries the plan out with the crew. It covers two real sites, each about 3.2 × 3.3 km at 1 m resolution, with up to 27 raster and 16 vector map layers per site:

  • Gale crater · Mount Sharp boxwork (Curiosity's site): sample a mineral-cemented boxwork ridge and two sandy hollows. Default plan: 1.92 km, 162 minutes in suits, GO.
  • Jezero crater · Three Forks sample depot (Perseverance's site): recover two of the sample tubes Perseverance left at Three Forks, then visit Wildcat Ridge and the Amalik outcrop on the delta front. Default plan: 2.57 km, 175 minutes in suits, GO.

Plan the walk. Routes run over a 2 m cost grid built from slope, metre-scale roughness, the chance of loose sand, and boulders. Walking speed comes from Tobler's hiking function, scaled for a suited astronaut and the load carried. Our own boulder detector finds about 4,400 boulders at Gale and 11,500 on Jezero's floor, and boulders of 2 m or more are no-go. Our sand model, built from THEMIS night infrared, HiRISE darkness and the USGS dune unit, scores an AUC of 0.84 against Jezero's mapped bedforms. Suggested science stops come from CRISM minerals, geologic contacts, ridge crests and rover sample sites, and each says why it is there. A pressurized rover (PR-2) can drive the crew to a drop-off: at Gale this halves the walking (1.92 to 0.88 km) and cuts time in suits from 162 to 127 minutes. Every limit is a slider (walking speed, slope, oxygen, battery, reserve, carried equipment), and each change replans the whole EVA in about a second.

Stay safe. The suit is simulated minute by minute for the planned walk and for the walk home from every point of it. The plan is GO only if the suit always holds enough for the walk back, times a tired-return factor, plus a reserve. The verdict comes with its reasons: the return margin on the limiting consumable, CO₂ against NASA's 20 mmHg contingency limit, sunset over the real horizon, radio line of sight, terrain, and space weather. Each NASA DONKI forecast of a CME reaching Mars is treated as a ±12-hour window. A hit during the EVA makes the plan NO-GO, and the planner offers the first clear start time. Caution and warning in the 3D console follows NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2: four alert classes with NASA's colours and tones, 28 monitored conditions and a turn-back clock. Every map layer carries a source tag (MEASURED, MAPPED, DERIVED, MODELED or RULE). Uncertainty is shown as ranges, and as a terrain-confidence layer where two independent terrain models disagree.

When something breaks. The ways-home layer draws the fastest walk back from every point as one network. It shows the gateways where many ways home meet and the ground with no way home. A suit-leak drill shows the ground that stays in reach as oxygen runs down. A partner-down drill finds the worst point of the route for an injured crew member. A cache planner puts oxygen caches where they do the most good: at Gale, three caches raise the share of ground within 30 minutes of a safe haven from 17 % to 72 %. There is no GPS on Mars, so a skyline fix matches the helmet's view of the horizon against the terrain model (median error 4 m at Gale, 17 m at Jezero). A HUD-failure drill leaves only a printed fallback card: heading, pace count, shadow clock and landmarks. Holding ABORT walks the crew home on the fastest route.

Plan smarter. "Plan it for me" builds safe, balanced and bold EVAs for a given time in suits. In the same 162 minutes as the hand-picked Gale plan it finds 1.3 times the science (1.4 times at Jezero). "Scout first" plans a helicopter flight over stretches where GO rests on uncertain data, as Ingenuity scouted for Perseverance. The flight's result is simulated, and the app says so. Crews can tag hazards and finds, see what each rock sample costs in minutes of margin, race a hand-drawn route against the planner, and follow pace notes read aloud along a strip map.

See the data together. A layer tower lifts every data layer off the terrain, each labelled with its mission and instrument, and a needle reads one point through all of them. Jezero's ancient lake can be flooded back to the levels published by Mangold et al. (2024). Perseverance's RIMFAX ground-penetrating radar (53 sols, about 7 km) hangs under its track as a curtain. Pins for 666 ChemCam and SuperCam laser-chemistry targets show what the rocks are made of. The app also shows Ingenuity's 24 flights over the site, plays Jezero's real wind recorded by SuperCam's microphone, and has an Earth link with the real light-time delay. The helmet streams EV1's position, suit and alerts live to the habitat console, and the habitat can push a waypoint into the visor.

Take it with you. "Then and now" puts you exactly where a rover's camera stood and wipes between its photo and our terrain rendered from the same pose. Arrival postcards show each stop before you reach it. An Apollo-style traverse sheet, a cuff checklist and a mission patch drawn from the route's own shape are ready to print. The site exports as a 3D-printable STL and as a GLB for phone AR. "Walk it on Earth" lets you walk the EVA at full scale on a sports field with your phone's GPS.

How it works

  • A Python pipeline builds each site from public products. It mosaics the HiRISE stereo terrain models, computes slope, roughness and the horizon from every 4 m cell, detects boulders, runs the sand model and lines CRISM up with HiRISE. It also adds the geology, rover tracks, chemistry, radar and a science score. A new site is one JSON file and one pipeline run.
  • A FastAPI backend with 68 endpoints does the planning: our directional A* route planner on a 2 m grid (cross-checked against scikit-image's Dijkstra), walk-back times by Dijkstra over reversed edges, and the suit simulation. It also handles radio line of sight with Mars' curvature, sunrise and sunset over the real horizon, space-weather windows, Mars time (our implementation of NASA GISS Mars24), the printables and the live link.
  • Two clients share one plan. The web planner (React and Leaflet) works on desktop, tablet and phone. The 3D console (Godot 4.7) has an orbit view for planning and a first-person helmet HUD for walking. It runs on a laptop with integrated graphics and takes keyboard, gamepad or offline voice commands, with glove-friendly controls.

How we checked it

  • Against the rovers' own drives: our walking map calls 97.8 % of Curiosity's 4.9 km and 99.8 % of Perseverance's 9.1 km inside the sites passable. No-go ground is 8 and 18 times rarer under the wheels than across each site.
  • As archived, CRISM's mineral maps sat 136-311 m off the HiRISE terrain. Each observation is now phase-correlated with the HiRISE mosaic, so the minerals sit on the right ground.
  • The rover teams' own terrain models agree with ours within half a metre after alignment.
  • The skyline fix is scored on 1,000 random points per site, and the Mars clocks are cross-checked against Mars24.
  • 203 automated tests (pytest), plus scripted check tours of the 3D console that include 25 NASA-standards checks.
  • The app lists its own limits under Data & method. For example, a 1 m terrain model cannot see rocks under about 1-2 m, and the weather is a climatology, not a forecast.

Benefits

  • Hyperlocal: one site at the scale of a single EVA, metre by metre, not region by region.
  • Safety first: a walk-back time for every point, consumable margins, GO or NO-GO with reasons, and drills for when things fail.
  • Honest data: every layer says where it comes from, uncertainty is shown, and the limits are listed.
  • The formats the challenge imagines: a habitat display, a tablet or phone app, a helmet HUD, and paper.

What we hope to achieve

We want to show what the first crews' EVA maps could look like: orbital and rover data fused at the scale of one walk, with safety you can see. The same tools could serve Mars analog field tests and classrooms today. With "Walk it on Earth", anyone can walk a real Mars EVA at full scale.

Tools, languages and software

Python 3.11 (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Rasterio, Shapely, Pillow), JavaScript (React 18, Leaflet, Zustand, Vite), Godot 4.7 with GDScript and 15 custom shaders, and pytest: about 45,000 lines of code. Built and run on a Windows laptop with integrated Intel graphics. The videos are screen recordings of the app, edited with ffmpeg, plus Blender renders in the 30-second demo (each labelled RENDER on screen).

Use of SI
